title: Blood Glucose Monitoring (POC)
summary: Point-of-care capillary blood glucose testing using a glucometer.
steps: Verify orders or protocol (frequency, target glucose range, sliding scale).
Perform hand hygiene and don gloves.
Turn on glucometer and insert test strip — confirm no error codes.
Have patient warm their hands or use the side of the fingertip for better blood flow.
Clean fingertip with alcohol swab. Allow to dry fully.
Lance the lateral aspect of the fingertip.
Apply gentle pressure to promote blood droplet. Wipe away first drop.
Touch second drop to test strip — do not smear.
Apply gauze to fingertip once sample collected.
Read result and compare to ordered parameters.
Administer insulin per sliding scale or notify provider if out of range.
Document result, time, and any interventions taken.
nursing_considerations: Rotate sites — lateral fingertips, avoid thumb and index finger.
Critical lows (<70) and highs (>400) require immediate intervention and provider notification.
Glucometer readings can be falsely low in severe hypoperfusion — confirm with venous glucose if concerned.
Change lancets each use — never reuse.
Document glucometer QC/calibration checks per facility policy.

title: Vital Signs Measurement
summary: Measuring and interpreting temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, SpO2, and pain.
equipment: Watch with second hand or timer
steps: Perform hand hygiene. Identify patient.
Temperature: Insert electronic thermometer per appropriate route. Normal: 97–99°F (36.1–37.2°C) oral. Report: >38.3°C (100.9°F) or <36°C (96.8°F).
Pulse: Palpate radial pulse for 60 seconds (if irregular) or 30 seconds × 2 (if regular). Note rate, rhythm, and strength. Normal: 60–100 bpm.
Respirations: Count breaths for 30 seconds × 2 while appearing to still take pulse (patients alter breathing when aware). Normal: 12–20 breaths/min.
SpO2: Apply pulse oximeter to finger (ensure good waveform). Normal: ≥95%. Alert: <92% or rapid drop.

Blood pressure: Position arm at heart level. Apply cuff over brachial artery (2–3 cm above antecubital fossa). Inflate 20–30 mmHg above palpated systolic. Deflate at 2 mmHg/second. Record Korotkoff sounds.
Normal BP: <120/80. Hypertension: ≥130/80. Hypotension: <90/60.
Assess pain using appropriate scale: 0–10 numeric, FACES scale, or CPOT for non-verbal patients.
Compare all values to the patient's baseline and previous readings.
Report significant changes: fever, HR >100 or <60, RR >20 or <12, SpO2 <92%, BP >160/100 or <90/60.
Document all values with time and any interventions.
nursing_considerations: Never take BP on an arm with an IV infusion, AV fistula, lymphedema, or recent mastectomy.
Orthostatic BP: measure supine, then standing at 1 and 3 minutes. >20 mmHg systolic drop = orthostatic hypotension.
Falsely low SpO2: poor perfusion, cold extremities, nail polish, motion — use earlobe or forehead probe as alternative.
Rectal temperature is the most accurate but invasive — use temporal or tympanic as alternatives.
Trending vital signs over time provides more clinical information than a single set of values.

title: Neurological Assessment & Glasgow Coma Scale
summary: Performing a focused neurological assessment including level of consciousness, GCS scoring, and cranial nerve evaluation.
steps: Introduce yourself. Assess level of consciousness (LOC) using AVPU: Alert, Verbal stimulation response, Painful stimulation response, Unresponsive.
Assess orientation: person, place, time, and situation (A&Ox4).
Perform Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS):
Eyes (E): Spontaneous = 4, To voice = 3, To pain = 2, None = 1.
Verbal (V): Oriented = 5, Confused = 4, Words = 3, Sounds = 2, None = 1.
Motor (M): Obeys commands = 6, Localizes pain = 5, Withdraws = 4, Abnormal flexion = 3, Extension = 2, None = 1.
Score: 15 = intact. 13–15 = mild impairment. 9–12 = moderate. ≤8 = severe — airway management indicated.
Assess pupils: size (mm), equality, and reaction to light (PERRL — Pupils Equal and Reactive to Light).
Normal: 2–6 mm, equal, brisk consensual response.
Fixed and dilated: herniation or atropine. Pinpoint: opiates, pontine lesion.
Assess cranial nerves as clinically indicated (smile for VII, tongue out for XII, shoulder shrug for XI).
Assess motor strength: grip strength bilateral, leg push/pull. Grade 0–5 scale.
Assess sensation: light touch and pain in extremities. Compare bilateral.
Assess coordination: finger-to-nose, heel-to-shin.
Document GCS score (with component scores), pupil response, motor strength, and any changes from baseline.
Report any changes: GCS decrease ≥2 points, unequal pupils, new focal deficits — immediate notification.
nursing_considerations: Sudden deterioration in neurological status (headache, vomiting, GCS drop) — notify provider STAT and prepare for emergent imaging.
GCS ≤8 is the threshold for considering airway protection — have airway equipment ready.
Do not attribute altered LOC to 'just sedation' without assessing — rule out physiological causes first.
Assess neuro checks at frequency ordered — for acute TBI or post-op craniotomy, checks may be every 15–30 minutes initially.
CIWA (alcohol withdrawal) and CPOT (pain in non-verbal patients) are specialized scales used alongside standard neuro checks.

title: Fall Risk Assessment (Morse Fall Scale)
summary: Evaluating a patient's fall risk using the Morse Fall Scale and implementing appropriate prevention measures.
steps: Complete Morse Fall Scale on admission, after falls, and per facility reassessment schedule.
Score the 6 Morse criteria:
History of falling (within 3 months): No = 0, Yes = 25.
Secondary diagnosis (≥2 medical diagnoses): No = 0, Yes = 15.
Ambulatory aid: None/bed rest/nurse assist = 0, Crutches/cane/walker = 15, Furniture = 30.
IV therapy/IV access: No = 0, Yes = 20.
Gait: Normal/bed rest/immobile = 0, Weak = 10, Impaired = 20.
Mental status: Knows own limits = 0, Forgets limitations = 15.
Total Score: 0–24 = No risk. 25–44 = Low risk. ≥45 = High risk.
Implement standard precautions for ALL patients: call light in reach, bed in lowest position, wheels locked.
For low-risk (25–44): ensure bed alarm, non-slip footwear, frequent rounding.
For high-risk (≥45): bed alarm ON, assistive device at bedside, fall risk band and signage, toilet/chair close, hourly rounding, consider chair alarm, educate patient and family.
Reassess after any change in condition, procedure, or medication change (sedatives, opioids, diuretics).
Document score, interventions, and patient/family education.
nursing_considerations: Falls are one of the most common inpatient adverse events — prevention requires consistent nursing surveillance, not just tools.
Patients often fall attempting to get to the bathroom — anticipate toileting needs and toilet before leaving the room.
Post-operative day 1 and medication changes (new opioids, sedatives, blood pressure meds) significantly increase fall risk.
Bed alarms do NOT prevent falls — they alert nurses after the patient is already moving to get up.
Never leave a high-fall-risk patient unattended when ambulating — use a gait belt and stay close.

title: Pain Assessment & Management
summary: Systematically assessing and documenting pain characteristics and evaluating effectiveness of interventions.
equipment: Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) 0–10 chart or FACES scale
steps: Assess pain routinely per facility schedule: on admission, every 4–8 hours, before and after analgesic administration.
Use appropriate pain scale:
NRS (0–10): 0 = no pain, 1–3 = mild, 4–6 = moderate, 7–10 = severe. Use for verbal, cognitively intact adults.
FACES scale: Use for pediatric patients or those with cognitive impairment who can point.
CPOT (Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool): Use for non-verbal or sedated patients. Scores facial expression, body movements, muscle tension, and ventilator compliance.
Characterize pain using PQRST: Precipitating/Palliating factors, Quality, Region/Radiation, Severity (score), Timing (onset, duration, pattern).
Assess impact: effect on activity, sleep, appetite, and mood.
Review current analgesic regimen and last administration time.
Implement non-pharmacologic interventions as appropriate: repositioning, ice/heat, distraction, relaxation.
Administer prescribed analgesics per order and reassess pain score 30–60 minutes after IV/IM, 60–90 minutes after oral.
If pain is uncontrolled: reassess trigger, contact provider, advocate for dose adjustment or rescue medication.
Document: pain score, location, quality, timing, interventions, and re-assessment score.
nursing_considerations: Pain is subjective — always believe the patient's self-report. Do not let vital signs or facial expression alone contradict self-reported pain.
Under-treating pain leads to physiological stress, delayed healing, and decreased patient satisfaction.
Over-treating with opioids causes sedation and respiratory depression — balance is key.
A pain score decrease of ≥2 points or 30–50% from baseline is generally considered clinically meaningful improvement.
Document reassessment after interventions — this is a regulatory and safety requirement, not optional.
